The Arkansas darter Etheostoma cragini is a small-bodied percid endemic to the Ozark highlands, where field surveys have documented that females attain sexual maturation at a standard length of 2.8 cm [Lp = 2.8 cm]. This size threshold for puberty represents a critical developmental milestone, marking the transition from somatic growth to reproductive investment in this short-lived species. At a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 15% [GSI = 15%]. The GSI was calculated from gravid females collected during the spring spawning season, when ovarian recrudescence reaches its peak. This figure falls within the range observed for other members of the subgenus Oligocephalus, suggesting a conserved pattern of reproductive investment among these benthic stream fishes.

Recent growth curve analyses based on otolith annuli and length-frequency distributions indicate that the ultimate standard length attained by Arkansas darter individuals is 5.2 cm [Li = 5.2 cm], a modest adult size typical of small-bodied darter species inhabiting upland streams. This asymptotic length corresponds to a total length of approximately 6 cm when converted using standard length-total length relationships derived for congeners. In comparison with other Etheostoma species occupying similar thermal regimes, this ultimate length is relatively constrained, likely reflecting the energetic limitations imposed by the cool, groundwater-fed streams that characterize the species' Ozark range. Field-collected specimens exceeding this length are exceptionally rare, suggesting that most individuals approach this asymptotic size within their first two years of life before growth decelerates markedly. The body size of this species has direct implications for its reproductive output and competitive interactions within the benthic fish assemblage.

Neonatal wet weight at birth for Etheostoma cragini is approximately 0.0012 g [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 g], a minute mass derived from the yolky eggs that measure roughly 1.3 mm in diameter. This estimate, calculated from the volume of a sphere of that diameter multiplied by an assumed tissue density, places the species among the smaller-bodied darter taxa in terms of per-offspring investment. The yolk-sac larvae that emerge following eclosion are lecithotrophic and depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. This initial mass represents a critical bottleneck in early life history, as the duration of yolk absorption and the timing of first feeding success directly influence larval survival rates. Field observations indicate that the pelagic larval phase is brief, with rapid settlement into benthic microhabitats occurring within days of hatching in the cool headwater streams.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Arkansas darters has been recorded as 2.7 g [Wwi = 2.7 g], a maximum body mass that reflects the species' small adult body size and its occupation of nutrient-limited stream environments. This value was estimated from the largest individuals encountered during intensive electrofishing surveys conducted across multiple seasons in the Spring River drainage. Comparisons with congeneric species reveal that this asymptotic mass is among the lowest recorded for the genus, consistent with the species' occurrence in cool, spring-fed habitats where productivity is inherently limited. The relationship between this ultimate mass and the 0.0012 g neonatal mass implies a substantial increase in body size over the lifespan, with growth concentrated in the first year post-hatching. This rapid early growth strategy is typical of short-lived darters that must reach reproductive size quickly given their constrained maximum longevity.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] that characterize many of the groundwater-fed streams inhabited by Etheostoma cragini, the maximum lifespan has been estimated at 1460 days [am = 1460 days], equivalent to approximately four years. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based aging of the oldest individuals encountered, places the species within the typical lifespan range for small-bodied darters of the Ozark region. The relatively short life expectancy imposes strong selective pressure for early maturation and high annual reproductive effort, a life-history syndrome reflected in the modest size at puberty of 2.8 cm standard length. Individuals that survive to the fourth year are rare, as most mortality occurs during the first year of life due to predation and the challenges of first-feeding success. This lifespan, combined with the species' small body size and documented fecundity, positions the Arkansas darter as an archetypal fast-lived, high-turnover component of the benthic fish community.
